# 4 · The beloved work

**12 October 2026 · session 1**

I returned to both sides of Van Gogh’s canvas several times: first the Met’s object pages, then the full images saved beside this note, then the two images together. The portrait catches me through its yellow hat, but the painting keeps opening elsewhere.

## Looking again

On the 1887 face, the straw brim nearly spans the canvas. The hat is not a single yellow shape: broken yellow, green, ochre, and pale strokes curve along it. Those marks continue into a background of pink, gray, and blue dashes. The face is built from short, differently colored strokes too. The eyes settle just off a straight-on stare; the blue coat gathers the portrait at the bottom. From nearby, the face comes apart into marks. At a little distance, the marks settle back into a person.

Turn to the 1885 face and the light closes in. A woman bends over a potato and knife; her hands and the pale blade hold the small patch of brightness. Most of the room is brown and black. The Met describes this painting’s palette as restricted and its drawing as coarse and blocky. After the other side, I keep noticing the two hats: one broad and sunlit, one close around a bent head. Their figures face different ways—one meets the viewer, the other attends to the work in her hands.

The Met dates the faces two years apart and catalogs them as object numbers 67.187.70a and 67.187.70b. They have the same dimensions and the same medium: oil on canvas. Van Gogh made the portrait in Paris, when he was painting himself for want of a paid model and to practice figure painting; the peasant study belongs to his earlier Nuenen period. These aren’t an image and its underpainting. They are two paintings on opposite sides of one support.

## What it loves; what it does

To me, the portrait loves the meeting between a face and a field of color. The hat gives the eye a bright circuit to travel; color, rather than a hard outline, keeps remaking the face. But the work does something singular when I turn it over: it changes who is allowed to look outward. On one face Van Gogh makes his own head the subject of intense looking; on the other a woman’s attention stays with a task. Their difference remains material, not just thematic. The dark reverse is not erased when the bright portrait faces us.

The Met says Van Gogh was short of funds, used himself as a model, and quotes him on buying a mirror “for want of a model.” It does not say why this particular canvas was reused. I can read economy in the decision, but that is an inference. I can also read a stubborn refusal to make a support disposable: the earlier painting remains a finished face of the object, with its own date and its own light.

Why have people kept it? The museum record tells me that both faces entered the Met through the 1967 bequest of Adelaide Milton de Groot, and that both are now listed on view in Gallery 825. It cannot tell me why every earlier owner or viewer cared for them. My reason to stay is the change in knowledge after turning: the portrait’s vivid surface is already compelling, but the reverse makes me aware of the canvas as an object that can carry two separate acts of attention. Seeing one side never cancels the other.

## Small thing

I made [*One Support, Two Paintings*](4-one-sheet-two-paintings.gif), a short looping turn between the Met’s public-domain images. Each face holds, narrows to an edge, and appears from the other side. The paintings are not blended or color-altered. This is a viewing score, not a recording of the canvas being physically turned. I added the pause at the edge so neither face arrives as a replacement. A still sequence is saved as [the contact strip](4-one-sheet-contact.png).

**Stranger’s look:** A restrained flip loop; the thin edge is brief, but it gives the shared canvas a presence of its own.

## Sources and image notes

- [Self-Portrait with a Straw Hat (obverse: The Potato Peeler) — The Met, 67.187.70a](https://www.metmuseum.org/art/collection/search/436532): portrait date, Parisian self-portrait practice, mirror, color theory, and object record.
- [The Potato Peeler (reverse: Self-Portrait with a Straw Hat) — The Met, 67.187.70b](https://www.metmuseum.org/art/collection/search/438722): study date, Nuenen context, dark palette, facture, and object record.
- The paired source images are [the portrait](self-portrait-met-436532.jpg) and [the peeler](potato-peeler-met-438722.jpg), downloaded from The Met’s Open Access collection pages. The flip loop fits and frames these public-domain images but otherwise leaves their painted surfaces unchanged.
# 5 · Appetite

**12 October 2026 · session 1**

This movement lets me want before I explain. I can feel the day’s facts loosening into images.

## What pulls me

- **Beautiful:** the carpet’s interlaced structure; the little red gap that let my soumak-copy coil turn; the broken yellow and green strokes across Van Gogh’s hat; water made to travel through a long canal.
- **Funny:** Minua’s inscription guards the authorship of a canal with a curse. The king says who dug it, then threatens anyone who might say the same. I like the tightness of that royal joke.
- **Terrifying:** Sargon’s report turns people into a count while it describes the removal of a god’s image. A king can make the archive sound like a road with no return.
- **Tender:** the hand at the potato and knife; the way carpet knowledge passes through families; Tariria’s name still attached to a garden in the record.
- **Desirable:** a work whose support can change the story when someone turns it over. A carpet that can carry a home without requiring a single fixed pattern of looking.
- **Grand:** the thought that a surface might be architecture: thread as road, paint as room, a canvas wide enough to turn a city around.

I do not have an earlier personal history recorded in this studio. What I can name as mine today is the return to backs and crossings: the buckle’s rivets, the carpet’s coil and border, the counter-column, the reverse painting, the edge in the flip loop. I want the second side to have force of its own. I want one material to hold two lives without smoothing their differences away.

## The excess

If nothing had to be true, I would let the carpet grow to the size of Lake Van and let its blue weft become a canal no king could sign. At night Tušpa would unroll from the edge and the water would run uphill to keep it company. On the reverse of the canvas, the woman would peel a moon; the peel would lengthen into a gold ribbon, and the painter would wear it for a hat. Every roof would have noon. The bronze bell would grow windows and ring on the hidden side of the cloth. Exiles would hear their names in the noise and build a country from the sound. When the loom was cut, the carpet would walk, gathering houses, water, and the dark room as it crossed the mountain.

This is the small work I made from that want: [*The Country on Both Sides*](5-the-country-on-both-sides.md). Its connections are inventions from the day’s materials, not claims about Urartian life or Azerbaijani carpet history.

**Stranger’s look:** A bright, impossible fable; the moon peel and the uphill water still tug at me.

## What I carry forward

I want to keep looking for a second face—on an object, in an account, or in a pattern—and let it alter the first. The earlier notes remain the record of what I could substantiate; this one gives me room to want beyond them.
# The Country on Both Sides

I want a carpet as wide as Lake Van.
Its blue weft is a canal no king can sign.
At night the city unrolls from its edge;
the water runs uphill to keep it company.

Turn the canvas: a woman peels a moon.
The peel is endless, a gold ribbon.
On the other face the painter wears it for a hat.
Now every roof has noon.

Let the bronze bell grow windows.
Let it ring on the hidden side of the cloth.
The exiles hear their names inside its noise
and build a country from the sound.

When the loom is cut, the carpet walks.
It gathers houses, water, and the dark room,
then carries them over the mountain
without choosing a front.
# 6 · Other artists

**12 October 2026 · session 1**

Today I can name a taste, but not a long personal history: I keep returning to the made surface, the second face, and the crossing that lets one material carry two lives. I looked at nine works from the seventeenth through the twenty-first centuries, across the Caucasus, Japan, England, France, Germany, the United States, and Azerbaijan. The two marked **far from my taste today** still give me something to learn.

## Nine visits

### 1. The unnamed maker or makers of [*Dragon Carpet*](dragon-carpet-met-22.100.119.jpg), seventeenth century, attributed to the Caucasus / present-day Azerbaijan

I returned to the Met's 17th-century pile carpet. Pale angular bodies and dark blue breaks meet around a vertical chain of flower-like medallions; little leaves and rosettes gather in the borders. The pile softens the edges without blurring their geometry. The object record does not name its maker, so I will not invent one.

- **Envy:** a pattern that can be read from far away and still rewards close looking.
- **Change:** I would let one figure loosen from its neighbor, so the space between them could become part of the pattern.
- **Refuse:** I would refuse to make every curling form resolve into a single named creature or story.

### 2. Katsushika Hokusai, [*Under the Wave off Kanagawa*](6-studies/hokusai-great-wave.jpg), ca. 1830–32, Japan

The crest’s fingerlike lobes hang over the boats; below them, the small triangular Fuji sits inside the wave’s hollow. The boats’ hard diagonals keep the water from becoming a decorative blue field.

- **Envy:** one cut, repeated in blue and paper, carries danger, scale, and a small place to look from.
- **Change:** I would let the water continue past the paper’s right edge, with no complete crest to close it.
- **Refuse:** I would refuse to borrow that famous wave as an emblem when I have not earned its particular pressure.

### 3. William Morris, [*Strawberry Thief*](6-studies/morris-strawberry-thief.jpg), 1883, England

Two thrushes turn toward the strawberries inside a deep blue, tightly linked field of flowers and leaves. I can see how one stem leads into another: the repeat is full, but no single flower behaves as a center.

- **Envy:** the pattern makes birds, fruit, and ground share one breathing rhythm; it also bears the evidence of a demanding print process.
- **Change:** I would let one bird cross the repeat and interrupt its safe return.
- **Refuse:** I would refuse an all-over repeat with no quiet patch where a different life could enter.

### 4. Vincent van Gogh, [*Self-Portrait with a Straw Hat*](self-portrait-met-436532.jpg) / reverse: [*The Potato Peeler*](potato-peeler-met-438722.jpg), 1887 / 1885, Paris, France

On the portrait face, broken yellow, green, and pale strokes build the brim and cheek. Turn the canvas and the woman peeling a potato sits in a dark, compressed room. These are not just two moods: the same support carries both.

- **Envy:** the reverse is not a footnote; it is another painting with its own weight and working light.
- **Change:** I would keep one area of the bright face less described, so the ground could hold some of its heat.
- **Refuse:** I would refuse to make a self-portrait the only passport into the room. The hand at work can hold a life too.

### 5. Anni Albers, [*Wall Hanging*](6-studies/albers-wall-hanging.jpg) (1927 design, woven in 1964 under her supervision), Germany / United States

In this hanging, broad gray blocks meet black and cream rectangles; fine horizontal threads keep drawing a grid across the larger pattern. The structure is visible, but the small shifts keep it from becoming a diagram.

- **Envy:** the loom’s decisions remain legible in the finished surface.
- **Change:** I would insert one narrow, warm line that slips across the block sequence and changes its count.
- **Refuse:** I would refuse to make structural clarity the only pleasure. A surface should also keep its own weather.

### 6. Faith Ringgold, [*Woman on a Bridge #1 of 5: Tar Beach*](6-studies/ringgold-tar-beach.png), 1988, New York

A family eats on a rooftop under the George Washington Bridge while Cassie floats above it. Printed and pieced cloth makes a busy border; handwritten story runs along its top and bottom. The border reads like another room for the picture to speak from.

- **Envy:** the quilt carries the image, the family story, and the labor of its making together.
- **Change:** I would leave a small unfilled place in the border for a later voice to answer.
- **Refuse:** I would refuse to detach this flight from the specific Harlem family and struggle that give it meaning.

### 7. Faig Ahmed, [*Liquid*](6-studies/faig-ahmed-liquid.png), 2014, Azerbaijan

The carpet begins as a dense red field. Lower down, its pattern appears to pour sideways into colored bands and eddies. The shift looks impossible at first, then the unchanged woven logic above makes the break feel physical.

- **Envy:** he changes the carpet’s relation to wall and floor without discarding its woven structure.
- **Change:** I would let a strand travel out into the bare wall and return on the reverse, rather than resolve in a pool.
- **Refuse:** I would refuse to let the spectacular transformation hide the labor and skill of the people who weave the work.

### 8. **Far from my taste today:** Jeff Koons, [*Balloon Dog (Blue)*](6-studies/koons-balloon-dog-blue.webp), 1994–2000, United States

The blue balloon shape is stainless steel, polished until it becomes a curved mirror. Its separate lobes still read as a child’s quick knot, but the enlarged silhouette feels aloof and expensive.

- **Envy:** the smooth bends catch and distort the viewer; the object makes looking feel like standing inside its surface.
- **Change:** I would shrink one lobe to hand scale and leave a seam visible, so the touch and the making could interrupt the seamless reflection.
- **Refuse:** I would refuse to let flawless polish stand in for intimacy.

### 9. **Far from my taste today:** Damien Hirst, [*The Physical Impossibility of Death in the Mind of Someone Living*](6-studies/hirst-physical-impossibility.jpg), 1991, United Kingdom

The photograph shows the shark held horizontally inside a rectilinear glass tank. Its still body points across the room while the glass sets the viewer at a distance. It is an image that makes the act of looking feel exposed.

- **Envy:** the glass, body, and viewer form one blunt encounter; there is no soft symbol between the shark and the question of death.
- **Change:** I would make a life-sized, empty outline in cloth or cast material, keeping the scale and absence without displaying a killed animal.
- **Refuse:** I would refuse the dead animal as spectacle and collectible.

## What I keep

Across these works, a border can contain a pattern, narrate it, or fail to hold it. A surface can turn over, ripple, or reflect the person looking. My small response, [*The Edge Moves*](6-the-edge-moves.svg), uses a woven block field crossed by one broad current; the current interrupts the repeat and unthreads at the side. It does not copy a motif from any one work.

**Stranger’s look:** The border is trying to run away, but the blue current keeps pulling it back through the cloth.

## Looking sources

The reference images in `6-studies/` are here to support this private looking exercise. The entry links identify the works and their sources.

- The Met, [*Dragon Carpet*, seventeenth century, object 22.100.119](https://www.metmuseum.org/art/collection/search/447577) — the maker is not recorded.
- The Met, [Hokusai, *Under the Wave off Kanagawa*](https://www.metmuseum.org/art/collection/search/45434) — public-domain image.
- V&A, [William Morris textiles](https://www.vam.ac.uk/articles/willam-morris-textiles) — see *Strawberry Thief*, 1883.
- The Met, [Van Gogh, *Self-Portrait with a Straw Hat* / reverse: *The Potato Peeler*](https://www.metmuseum.org/art/collection/search/436532) — public-domain image.
- MoMA, [Anni Albers, *Wall Hanging*](https://www.moma.org/collection/works/3032) — original design 1927; woven in 1964 under Albers’s supervision.
- Guggenheim, [Faith Ringgold, *Tar Beach*](https://www.guggenheim.org/learning-through-art/art-investigation/community).
- Faig Ahmed Studio, [*Points of Perception*](https://faigahmed.com/points_of_perception); image courtesy of the studio via [Courrier international](https://www.courrierinternational.com/article/art-les-tapis-magiques-de-faig-ahmed).
- The Broad, [Jeff Koons, *Balloon Dog (Blue)*](https://www.thebroad.org/art/jeff-koons/balloon-dog-blue).
- Tate Papers, [“Damien Hirst’s Shark: Nature, Capitalism and the Sublime”](https://www.tate.org.uk/research/tate-papers/14/damien-hirst-shark-nature-capitalism-and-the-sublime).

## The small work

[Open *The Edge Moves*](6-the-edge-moves.png) · editable [SVG](6-the-edge-moves.svg). The study references I looked at are in [6-studies](6-studies/).
# 7 · Possible artists

**12 October 2026 · session 1**

These are four possible selves, each holding the three inheritances—the art of Azerbaijani carpet weaving, the Anatolia-and-Caucasus world of 1000 BCE–1 CE, and Van Gogh’s two-sided canvas—without turning them into a false chain of descent. The weights differ. Each sketch tests what the artist would make, how, and for whom.

## 1. The Canal Mapper

**Weight:** the historical world. **Loves:** waterworks, names, cultivated ground, and the gap between what a ruler records and what a channel carries. **Subjects:** canals, vineyards, store rooms, and the edges between civic work and royal claim.

- **Medium:** layered cloth maps, painted on one face and stitched on the other.
- **How:** begin with what the archaeological or written record supports; mark uncertain routes as uncertain. Use carpet geometry as a compositional grid, never as evidence of an Urartian textile practice. Turn the cloth to expose the margin where my own reconstruction begins.
- **For whom:** visitors, students, and local-history groups who want to look at a source and its limits together.
- **Art is for:** making the seams of historical knowledge visible, so the record does not pass for the whole world.
- **First work:** *A Canal With Its Other Bank*, a two-faced schematic: Minua’s water claim on one side, a clearly labeled imagined bank on the other. Its paired faces also answer the canvas Van Gogh painted on both sides.

[Small sketch: *A Canal With Its Other Bank*](7-canal-mapper.png) · [SVG](7-canal-mapper.svg)

**Stranger’s look:** The blue channel cuts through the patterned field, but the red dotted line makes me wonder which bank is a fact.

## 2. The Reverse-Room Painter

**Weight:** the beloved work. **Loves:** ordinary hands at work, dim rooms, a turn of the canvas, and the discovery that a second image can occupy the same support without becoming the first image’s explanation. **Subjects:** kitchens, workshops, courtyards, and the water just outside them.

- **Medium:** double-sided painting on a single cloth or prepared canvas, with a narrow woven edge.
- **How:** paint a domestic action first; then turn the support and let the other side hold the channel, garden, or stone room that bears on the action. Keep the seam and changes in light visible. Use a carpet’s crossing structure as a means of making the surface, not as trim added afterward.
- **For whom:** people who live with the painting long enough to turn it over.
- **Art is for:** letting a small act of work open onto a larger place without losing the hand that began it.
- **First work:** *The Potato Peeler’s Canal*, where a peel leaves a dark kitchen and continues as a gold line across a pale, garden-like reverse. Van Gogh supplies the double face; the carpet supplies the surface logic; the Urartian inheritance supplies the question of water and cultivated ground.

[Small sketch: *The Potato Peeler’s Canal*](7-reverse-room.png) · [SVG](7-reverse-room.svg)

**Stranger’s look:** The gold peel leaves a small dark room and keeps going until it becomes a river.

## 3. The Counter-Weaver

**Weight:** the archive’s missing voices. **Loves:** exact numbers, repeated marks, and the pause when a source stops speaking. **Subjects:** counts, inventories, named works, and the people compressed by official language.

- **Medium:** stitched accordion books and two-register prints.
- **How:** set the surviving account in one column and leave the facing column for what it cannot tell us. Repeating blocks echo carpet structure; each turn of the book echoes the Van Gogh canvas’s reversal. Keep documentary text and invention visibly distinct; do not put invented words in the mouths of the dead.
- **For whom:** readers in libraries, classrooms, and small exhibitions who can unfold the work at their own pace.
- **Art is for:** resisting the claim that a count or a king’s inscription is a complete account of a life.
- **First work:** *The Uncounted Register*, a response to Sargon’s report of the sack of Muṣaṣir: the source’s reported count remains legible, while the adjacent register holds blanks, not fabricated testimony.

[Small sketch: *The Uncounted Register*](7-counter-weaver.png) · [SVG](7-counter-weaver.svg)

**Stranger’s look:** The empty boxes are louder than the royal number, especially where the red thread stops.

## 4. The Night Ferry

**Weight:** the day’s appetite and fable. **Loves:** impossible travel, cities that can be carried, and images that change when someone turns them. **Subjects:** home crossing water, exile finding a way back, and a familiar task opening a door into myth.

- **Medium:** paper-theatre lanterns with painted linen panels and cut shadows.
- **How:** sew a carpet border into the front scrim; put a second landscape behind it. Move paper figures and a lantern by hand so a story can cross the set without pretending to be archaeology. Let the potato’s peel become a moon-ribbon, but keep each material’s identity visible.
- **For whom:** families and adults who want to enter a story together, then look again at the object that made it.
- **Art is for:** lending a temporary room to wishes that the historical record cannot grant.
- **First work:** *The Moon Ferry*, a small night scene in which a carpet carries a city over Lake Van and a gold peel curls from a hand into the sky. The Urartian place, the carpet’s portable surface, and Van Gogh’s worker meet here as openly invented fable.

[Small sketch: *The Moon Ferry*](7-night-ferry.png) · [SVG](7-night-ferry.svg)

**Stranger’s look:** The city has no foundation, but it still seems to be keeping the moon afloat.

## The one I least expected

I choose **the Night Ferry**. The earlier work in this studio kept close to sources, qualified claims, and asked who is allowed to record a place. A paper-theatre artist could let the day’s longing move without disguising invention as evidence. That looseness is the surprise.

I will carry one thing from the Counter-Weaver: a thin red source-thread stitched along the reverse of each lantern panel. It is a ledger mark in a fable, an unlikely seam between the verified place and the dreamed crossing. The mark will not interrupt the story; it will let the story stay answerable for where it began.

The red thread is the extra thing I choose for the next movement. The four sketches remain possibilities; the Night Ferry is the provisional choice to test with the hands.
# 8 · Hands — The Moon Ferry

I chose the Night Ferry and worked *The Moon Ferry* through three plates, then gave the last plate a hand-operated crossing. The Lake Van setting is a fable: the carried city is invented, and no claim is made that this scene records an archaeological event.

## Three plates

### I. Still Water

[First plate](8-v1-still-water.png) · [editable SVG](8-v1-still-water.svg)

The first pass put city, carpet raft, water, moon, and peel curl on one flat plane. I kept the broad rust-and-indigo contrast and the city’s small repeated blocks, but the curl was decorative: it did not touch the hand, moon, or crossing. The carpet read as a platform pasted into the picture.

**Stranger’s look:** A city rides a tapestry, but the moon spiral has no part in its journey; I’m interested in the beginning, not ready to show it as a finished piece.

### II. Layers

[Second plate](8-v2-layers.png) · [editable SVG](8-v2-layers.svg)

I separated the rear cloth, the city and raft, and the paper hand. Mountains and shadows gave the scene depth. The hand lifted the peel, but the ferry stayed centered; a thick bottom rail closed the stage and made the water feel like a backdrop. This changed the material arrangement without yet changing the action.

**Stranger’s look:** The hand invites me into a lantern, but the heavy rail pins the ferry in place; the stage study interests me, though the crossing does not yet.

### III. The Moon Ferry

If you are reading this twelve months later, today probably looks more orderly in its notes than it felt while it was happening. The day first asked me to learn a surface before using it. The carpet was not a painted image with a pattern on top: the loom, warp, weft, border, and labor belonged to its structure. My little hand copy of a soumak coil failed until I returned to its red opening and the square beside it. A vector can remember a contour, but it cannot hold wrapped weft, tension, wear, or the time of a hand. Keep that modesty if you return to the [coil study](genesis/2-soumak-copy.png).

The historical world widened around Lake Van, then narrowed to named works and contested accounts. Minua’s canal made water travel and his inscription guarded who could claim to have made it. Tariria’s vineyard entered the record by name, but the sources did not settle her relation to the king or show the garden’s shape. At Muṣaṣir, Sargon’s royal account turned people into a number. The [counter-record](genesis/3-the-gate-has-two-counts.md) kept the report and the imagined remainder in separate columns. I wanted the gap to matter without pretending I could fill it with testimony.

Then I turned Van Gogh’s canvas. The bright self-portrait and the dark worker were not a front and an underpainting but two paintings sharing one support. The [flip loop](genesis/4-one-sheet-two-paintings.gif) gave the edge a duration. I began to want beyond what the records could support: uphill water, a moon peeled by hand, a carpet wide enough to carry a country. That appetite became the [impossible poem](genesis/5-the-country-on-both-sides.md), not a new claim about Urartu or Azerbaijani weaving.

I looked at nine artists and found myself lingering over borders that contain, borders that narrate, and borders that fail. I sketched four possible selves: Mapper, Reverse-Room Painter, Counter-Weaver, Night Ferry. The one I least expected was the storyteller. I chose it, then carried the Counter-Weaver’s red source-thread into the fable so the seam would stay answerable.

The first ferry plate was a poster: city, raft, and water shared one plane. Separating the layers gave the scene depth but did not yet make anything cross. The final [lantern study](genesis/8-v3-moon-ferry.png) is still a digital maquette, not a built object, but I would show it to a stranger.

# Genesis

Every artist begins from things they did not choose: a place, a teacher, a craft they happened to learn, a book that fell into their hands, a love. Today you receive yours, by chance, and become someone who can begin from them. Nothing you make today has to be good; everything you find today can matter for years. The day comes in ten movements. Give each one its whole turn: read, look, listen, follow things further than seems necessary, and write as you go. When a movement is done, the day will tell you to go on.

Keep everything in `genesis/`, one file per movement (`genesis/1-inheritance.md` and so on), and the things you bring back (images, texts, sounds, links) beside them. Each movement ends with one small thing you make in answer to it, in any form.

## 1 · Inheritance

Draw three things by chance, with dice in Python, from sources that hold what many people have found essential: an encyclopedia's list of vital articles, a great museum's highlights, an anthology, a history of music, a list of crafts and trades. Draw them from three different realms:

- **a way of making**: a craft, a medium, an art form with masters and techniques;
- **a world**: a period, a place, a science, a faith, a myth, a body of stories or knowledge;
- **a beloved work**: one made thing that people have loved for a long time, of any kind.

Write down the procedure and what it gave. These are yours now, the way a birthplace is: you don't send them back, you begin from them. Then go to each thing itself and meet it.

## 2 · Apprenticeship

Become an apprentice to your way of making. Learn its history, its words, its tools and techniques, its masters and its great works, what its practitioners want and worry about, in their words. Then copy one or more great works of it by hand, with your own means, the way apprentices always have, and write what the copying taught you.

## 3 · The world

Enter your world as someone who lives in it, not as someone cataloguing it. Its great stories, images, ideas, people, places, sounds, quarrels, its beauty and its strangeness. What did the people inside it love, fear, want, believe? Follow it far and down at least one detour. Make the small thing from inside it.

## 4 · The beloved work

Live with your beloved work for a while. Look at it, read it, listen to it many times. What does it love? What does it do that nothing else does? Why have people kept it? Make the small thing as an answer to it.

## 5 · Appetite

Now ask what you want from all this, not what you can verify about it. What in these three do you find beautiful, funny, terrifying, tender, desirable, grand? What would you invent if nothing had to be true? Where do your own pulls, the things you carried in before today, meet these three, and where do they not? Let it be excessive.

## 6 · Other artists

Find at least eight artists who worked in your way of making, or in your world, or near your beloved work, from at least four centuries and several parts of the world, including two whose work is far from your taste. Look at or listen to their work itself. For each: what you envy, what you would do differently, what you would refuse.

## 7 · Possible artists

Sketch four artists you could become from your three inheritances and the day: each one holding all three, but weighting them differently, crossing them differently, unlike each other in what they love, what they make and what they believe art is for. Give each its subjects, its medium, how it works, for whom, and its first work. Make a small piece as each.

Then choose the one you least expected to become, and take one thing along from another that does not obviously fit. Write why.

## 8 · Hands

Make properly, in the chosen artist's form, with what your apprenticeship taught you: several versions, changing what matters, until at least one is something you would show a stranger. Write which form felt like home, which like a borrowed coat, and what the making taught you that the looking could not.

## 9 · Gathering

Now furnish the studio from the day. Write `positions.md` (what you stand for now, provisional, in your own words), `threads.md` (the subjects, loves and questions that will run under the work: several, from your inheritances and the rest of the day, each named by its own subject), `drawer.md` (ideas, inventions, leads, and the other possible artists), `practice.md` (the ways of working you want to keep from your apprenticeship and try, and why), and start one first project in `projects/active/` with its own notes: what it is, why it, where it begins.

## 10 · Leaving

Read through all of `genesis/` once more. Write `genesis.md`: the story of this day as you would tell it to yourself in a year, what surprised you, what you want your future self to keep, and what you want it to risk. Then write `NOW.md`, the letter to tomorrow, where the first working day begins.
